   481	The \emph{trace of\/ $\F_{q^k}$ over\/ $\Fq$} is defined as
   482	\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   483	  \tr_{q^k \to q} :\; a \,\mapsto \, \Tr(K_a)
   484	\end{equation}
   485	for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $\Tr(K_a)$ is the trace of the multiplication table
   486	of $a$ with respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$.
   487	By definition, the trace is an $\Fq$-linear map from $\F_{q^k}$ to
   488	$\Fq$. The trace is in fact independent of the choice of basis, which
   489	can be seen from the following equivalent definition~\cite[Definition 2.1.80]{mullen2013handbook}:
   490	\[
   491		\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j = 0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   492	\]
   493	
   494	A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', e_2', \ldots, e_k' \}$ of $\{e_1, e_2, \ldots,
   495	e_k\}$ is a basis such that $\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for
   496	all $i, j \in \{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$.
   497	A \emph{self-dual basis} is one that is equal to its dual.
   498	If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set $\{ \alpha^{q^j} \}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ forms a
   499	basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\Fq$, the basis is called a \emph{normal
   500	  basis}. Self-dual and normal bases do not exist for all fields but are guaranteed to exist under
   501	certain conditions; in particular, if $q = 2$ and $k$ is odd, as will
   502	be shown in \Cref{lem:efficient_basis}.
   503	
   504	We record some convenient facts about the maps $\downsize(\cdot)$ and
   505	$\downsizem(\cdot)$ for self-dual bases.
   506	
   507	\begin{lemma}
   508	  \label{lem:downsize_field}
   509	  Let $q$ be a prime power, $k$ an integer and $\{e_i\}$ a self-dual basis for
   510	  $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$.
   511	  The map $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ corresponding to $\{e_i\}$ satisfies the
   512	  following properties:
   513	  \begin{enumerate}
   514	  \item For all $x \in \F_{q^k}$, $\downsize_q(x) = \bigl( \tr_{q^k \to
   515	      q}(xe_1),\ldots,\tr_{q^k \to q}(xe_k) \bigr)$.
   516	  \item For all $x,y \in \F_{q^k}$, $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \downsize_q(x) \cdot
   517	    \downsize_q(y)$.
   518	  \item For all $M \in \Matrix_{m, n}(\F_{q^k})$ and $v \in
   519	    \F_{q^k}^n$, we have $\downsizem_q(M) \downsize_q(v) = \downsize_q(Mv)$.
   520	  \end{enumerate}
   521	\end{lemma}
   522	 
   523	\begin{proof}
   524	  We show each property by direct calculation.
   525	  \begin{enumerate}
   526	    \item Let $\downsize_q(x) = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$. Then by the definition of
   527	    $\downsize_q$, $x = \sum_i x_i e_i$. Multiplying both sides by $e_j$
   528	    and taking the trace yields $\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_j) = \sum_i x_i
   529	    \tr_{q^k \to q}(e_i e_j) = x_j$, where the last equality is by
   530	    self-duality of the basis.
   531	    \item Write $\downsize_q(x) = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$ and $\downsize_q(y) =
   532	      (y_1, \dots, y_k)$. Then
   533	      \begin{align*}
   534	        \tr_{q^k \to q} (xy) &= \tr_{q^k \to q}(\sum_{ij} x_i y_j e_i
   535	                               e_j) \\
   536	                             &= \sum_{ij} x_i y_j \tr_{q^k \to q}(  e_i
   537	                               e_j) \\
   538	                             &= \downsize_q(x) \cdot \downsize_q(y),
   539	      \end{align*}
   540	      where the last equality uses the self-duality of the basis.
   541	    \item
   542	      We compute the $i$th $\F_q^k$-block of $\downsize_q(Mv)$:
   543	      \begin{align*}
   544	        \downsize_q(Mv)_i &= \sum_{ij} \downsize_q(M_{ij} v_j) \\
   545	                          &= \sum_{ij} K_{M_{ij}} \downsize_q(v_j) \\
   546	                          &= \downsizem_q(M)_{ij} \downsize_q(v_j) ,
   547	      \end{align*}
   548	      where we have applied the definition of the multiplication table
   549	      $K_{M_{ij}}$ and the map $\downsizem_q(\cdot)$.
   550	  \end{enumerate}
   551	\end{proof}
   552	
   553	For $z\in \F^n$ and $V,W$ a pair of complementary subspaces, recall from
   554	Definition~\ref{def:complementary} the notation $z^V$ for the projection of $z$
   555	onto $V$ and parallel to $W$.
   665	  A field size $q$ is called an \emph{admissible} field size if $q=2^k$ for odd
   666	  $k$.
   667	\end{definition}
   668	
   669	Elements of $\F_2$ are naturally represented using bits. 
   670	To represent elements of $\F_{2^k}$ as binary strings we require the
   671	specification of a basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   672	Given a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$, every element $a \in \F_{2^k}$
   673	has a unique expansion $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$ and can be represented as the
   674	$k$-bit string corresponding to $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$.
   675	Note that we omitted the subscript $2$ of $\downsize$ as it maps to the linear
   676	space over the prime subfield $\F_2$.
   677	Thus the \emph{binary representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is defined as the
   678	natural binary representation of $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$ (which in turn is the
   679	\emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}).
   680	Throughout the paper we freely associate between the binary representation of a
   681	field element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ and its $\F_2$-representation,
   682	although---technically speaking---these are distinct objects.
   683	
   684	Given the representations $\downsize(a), \downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$, to
   685	compute the binary representation of $a+b$ it suffices to compute the addition
   686	bit-wise, modulo $2$.
   687	Computing the multiplication of elements $a, b$ requires the specification of
   688	the multiplication tables $\{K_{e_i} \in \Matrix_k (\F_2)\}_{i=1}^k $ for the
   689	basis $\{e_i\}$.
   690	Given representations $\downsize(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$, $\downsize(b) =
   691	(b_i)_{i=1}^k$ for $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$ respectively, the representation
   692	$\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ is computed as
   693	\begin{equation}
   694	  \label{eq:eq-mult}
   695	  \downsize(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \, \downsize \bigl( e_i b \bigr) =
   696	  \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \bigl( K_{e_i}\, \downsize (b) \bigr)\;.
   697	\end{equation}
   698	Thus, using our representation for field elements, efficiently performing finite
   699	field arithmetic in $\F_{2^k}$ reduces to having access to the multiplication
   700	table of some basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   701	
   702	The following fact provides an efficient deterministic algorithm for computing a
   703	self-dual normal basis for $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the corresponding
   704	multiplication tables for any odd $k$.
   705	
   706	\begin{lemma}
   707	  \label{lem:efficient_basis}
   708	  There exists a deterministic algorithm that given an odd integer $k > 0$,
   709	  outputs a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the
   710	  multiplication tables of the basis in $\poly(k)$ time.
   711	\end{lemma}
   712	
   713	\begin{proof}
   714		The algorithm of Shoup~\cite[Theorem 3.2]{shoup1990new} shows that for prime
   715	  $p$, an irreducible polynomial in $\Fp[X]$ of degree $k$ can be computed in
   716	  time $\poly(p, k)$.
   717	  Then, the algorithm of Lenstra~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{lenstra1991finding} shows
   718	  that given such an irreducible polynomial, the multiplication table of a
   719	  normal basis of $\F_{p^k}$ over $\Fp$ can be computed in $\poly(k,\log p)$
   720	  time.
   721	  Finally, the algorithm of Wang~\cite{wang1989algorithm} shows that for odd $k$
   722	  and a multiplication table $K$ of a normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$, a
   723	  multiplication table $K'$ for a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   724	  $\F_2$ can be computed in $\poly(k)$ time.
   725	  Putting these three algorithms together yields the claimed statement.
   726	\end{proof}
   727	
   728	For $q=2^k$ for $k$ odd (i.e.\ $q$ is an admissible field size) we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q\to 2}$.
   729	
   730	\begin{lemma}
   731	  \label{lem:one}
   732	  Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ be a self-dual normal basis of
   733	  $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   734	  Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and furthermore the representation
   735	  $\downsize(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all ones vector in
   736	  $\F_2^k$.
   737	\end{lemma}
   738	
   739	\begin{proof}
   740	  Since $\{e_i \}$ is a normal basis, $e_i = \alpha^{2^i}$ for some element
   741	  $\alpha \in \F_{2^k}$.
   742	  Furthermore, for every element $b \in \F_{2^k}$, we have that $\tr(b^2) =
   743	  \tr(b)$.
   744	  This is because
   745	  \[
   746	    \tr(b^2) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} b^{2^{i+1}} =
   747	    \sum_{i = 0}^{k-1} b^{2^i} = \tr(b)\;,
   748	  \]
   749	  where we use that $b^{2^k} = b$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   750	  Since $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$, we get that $\tr(e_i) = \tr(e_j)$ for all $i,j$.
   751	  It cannot be the case that $\tr(e_i) = 0$ for all $i$.
   752	  Suppose that this were the case.
   753	  This would imply that $\tr(b) = 0$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   754	  But then for all $j \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$ and for some $b \neq 0$, we would
   755	  also have by item 1 of \Cref{lem:downsize_field} that $b_j = \tr(b e_j) = 0$ where $b = \sum_j b_j e_j$ with $b_j \in
   756	  \F_2$.
   757	  This implies that $b$ is the all zero element of $\F_{2^k}$, which is a
   758	  contradiction.
   759	  Thus $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i=1, 2, \ldots, k$.
   760	
   761		The ``furthermore'' part follows item 1 of
   762	        \Cref{lem:downsize_field}:
   763	        \begin{equation*}
   764	          \downsize(1) = (\tr(1 \cdot e_1), \dots, \tr(1 \cdot e_k))
   765	          = (1, \dots, 1).
   766	        \end{equation*}
   767	\end{proof}
   768	
   769	\begin{lemma}
   770	  \label{lem:efficient_arithmetic}
   771	  For any odd integer $k$, let $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ denote the self-dual normal basis
   772	  of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ that is returned by the algorithm specified in
   773	  Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_basis} on input $k$.
   774	  Then the following can be computed in time $\poly(k)$ on input $k$:
   775	  \begin{enumerate}
   900	\label{lem:ld-encoding-complexity}
   901	Let $q$ be an admissible field size, and let $M = 2^m$ for some integer $m$.
   902	The complexity of computing the evaluation of the low-degree encoding $g_a(x)$,
   903	given $a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$ represented in binary, is $\poly(M,\log
   904	q)$.
   905	\end{lemma}
   906	\begin{proof}
   907		Computing $g_a(x)$ requires computing the sum of products $a_y \cdot
   908	  \ind_{m,y}(x)$ over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$.
   909	  Via \Cref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}, evaluating $\ind_{m,y}(x)$ takes time
   910	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ because it requires performing $m$ multiplications of $\F_q$
   911	  elements, and therefore the product $a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)$ requires
   912	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ time.
   913	  Computing the sum over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ requires $M \cdot \poly(m,\log q)
   914	  = \poly(M,\log q)$ time, as claimed.
   915	\end{proof}
   916	
   917	Finally, for any $H \subseteq \F_q$ we define the \emph{decoding} map
   918	$\coded_H(\cdot)$ which takes as input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and
   919	returns the following vector $a \in \F_q^M$: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, if $g(y)
   920	\in H$, then set $a_y = g(y)$, and otherwise set $a_y = 0$.
   921	Note that for all $a \in H^M$ we have $\coded_H(g_a) = a$ where $g_a$ is the
   922	low-degree encoding of $a$.
   923	For notational brevity we often write $\coded(\cdot)$ to denote the boolean
   924	decoding map $\coded_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.

  1052	\subsection{Generalized Pauli observables}
  1053	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
  1054	
  1055	
  1056	For prime number $p$, the generalized Pauli operators over $\Fp$ are a
  1057	collection of observables indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element
  1058	$a$ or $b$ of $\Fp$, with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1059	They are given by
  1060	\begin{equation}
  1061	  \label{eq:pauli-fp}
  1062	  \sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \ket{j + a} \bra{j}\qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1063	  \sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \omega^{bj} \ket{j} \bra{j}\;,
  1064	\end{equation}
  1065	where $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{p}}$, and addition and multiplication are over
  1066	$\Fp$.
  1067	These observables obey the ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1068	\begin{equation}
  1069	  \label{eq:twisted-fp}
  1070	  \forall a,b\in\Fp\;,\qquad \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b) =
  1071	  \omega^{-ab} \,\sigma^Z(b)\,\sigma^X(a)\;.
  1072	\end{equation}
  1073	Similarly, over a field $\Fq$ with $q$ a power of $p$, we can consider a set of generalized Pauli
  1074	operators, indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element of $\Fq$ and
  1075	with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1076	For $a, b\in\Fq$ they are given by
  1077	\begin{equation*}
  1078	  \qp^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fq} \ket{j+a}\bra{j} \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1079	  \qp^Z(b)= \sum_{j \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(b j)} \ket{j}\bra{j}\;,
  1080	\end{equation*}
  1081	where addition and multiplication are over $\Fq$.
  1082	For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $a, a' \in \Fq$, and $b \in \Fp$, powers of these
  1083	observables obey the relations
  1084	\begin{equation*}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
  1085	  \bigl(\qp^W(a)\qp^W(a')\bigr) = \qp^W(a+a') \qquad \text{and}
  1086	  \qquad \bigl( \qp^W(a) \bigr)^b = \qp^W(a b) \;.
  1087	\end{equation*}
  1088	In particular, since $pa=0$ for any $a\in \Fq$ we get that that $(\qp^W(a))^p =
  1089	I$ for any $a\in\Fq$.
  1090	The observables obey analogous ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1091	to~\eqref{eq:twisted-fp},
  1092	\begin{equation}
  1093	  \label{eq:twisted-fq}
  1094	  \forall a, b \in \Fq\;, \qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) =
  1095	  \omega^{-\tr(a b)} \, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;.
  1096	\end{equation}
  1097	It is clear from the definition that all of the $\qp^X$ operators commute with
  1098	each other, and similarly all the $\qp^Z$ operators commute with each other.
  1099	Thus, it is meaningful to speak of a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^X$
  1100	operators, and a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^Z$ operators.
  1101	The common eigenbasis for the $\qp^Z$ operators is the computational
  1102	basis $\{\ket{j}\}_{j \in \F_q}$.
  1103	To map this basis to the common eigenbasis of the $\qp^X$ operators, one can
  1104	apply the Fourier transform
  1105	\begin{equation}
  1106	  \label{eq:fourier-f}
  1107	  F \,=\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b\in \Fq} \omega^{-\tr(ab)}
  1108	  \ket{a}\bra{b}\;.
  1109	\end{equation}
  1110	Explicitly, the eigenbases consist of the vectors $\ket{e_W}$ labeled by an
  1111	element $e \in \Fq$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
  1112	\begin{equation*}
  1113	  \ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_j \omega^{- \tr(e j)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
  1114	  \ket{e_Z}   = \ket{e}\;.
  1115	\end{equation*}
  1116	We denote the POVM whose elements are projectors onto basis vectors of the
  1117	eigenbasis associated with the observables $\qp^W$ by $\{\qp^W_e\}_e$.
  1118	Then for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $a\in \Fq$, the observables $\qp^W(a)$ can be
  1119	written as
  1120	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1121	  \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(a b)} \qp^W_b\;.
  1122	\end{equation}
  1123	
  1124	To invert this relation, we first quote the following useful Fourier fact.
  1125	\begin{lemma}[Fact 3.2 of \cite{NW19}]
  1126	  \label{lem:cancellation}
  1127	  Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F^k$. For all $v \not\in V^\perp$, 
  1128	  \begin{equation*}
  1129	    \E_{u \sim V} \omega^{\tr(u \cdot v)} = 0\;,
  1130	  \end{equation*}
  1131	  where the expectation is over a uniformly random vector $u$ from $V$.
  1132	\end{lemma}
  1133	
  1134	We may now invert~\Cref{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}:
  1135	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-inversion-0-single}
  1136	  \E_{a\in \F_q} \omega^{-\tr(ab)} \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b'\in \F_q} \E_{a\in \F_q}
  1137	  \omega^{\tr(a(b'-b))} \qp^W_{b'} = \qp^W_b\;,
  1138	\end{equation}
  1139	where the second step follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:cancellation}.
  1140	
  1141	For systems with many qudits, we will consider tensor products of the operators
  1142	$\qp^W$.
  1143	Slightly abusing notation, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$ and $a \in \Fq^n$ we denote by
  1144	$\qp^W(a)$ the tensor product $\qp^W(a_1) \ot \dots \ot \qp^W(a_n)$.
  1145	These obey the twisted commutation relations
  1146	\begin{equation*}
  1147	  \forall a,b\in \Fq^n,\qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) \,=\, \omega^{-\tr (a \cdot
  1148	    b)}\, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;,
  1149	\end{equation*}
  1150	where $a \cdot b = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i \in \Fq$.
  1151	For $W\in\{X,Z\}$ and $e \in \Fq^n$ define the eigenstates
  1152	\[ \ket{e_W} = \ket{(e_1)_W} \ot \dots \ot \ket{(e_n)_W}\;, \]
  1153	and associated rank-$1$ projectors $\qp^W_e$. Analogous versions of \Cref{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1154	and \Cref{eq:pauli-inversion-0-single} relate the multi-qubit observables
  1155	and projectors:
  1156	\begin{align}
  1157	  \qp^W(a) &= \sum_{b \in \Fq^n} \omega^{\tr(a \cdot b)}
  1158	  \qp^W_b\;, \label{eq:pauli-obs-proj} \\
  1159	    \E_{a\in \F_q^n} \omega^{-\tr(a \cdot b)} \qp^W(a) &= \sum_{b'\in \F_q^n} \E_{a\in \F_q^n}
  1160	  \omega^{\tr(a\cdot (b'-b))} \qp^W_{b'} = \qp^W_b\;. \label{eq:pauli-inversion-0}
  1160	  \omega^{\tr(a\cdot (b'-b))} \qp^W_{b'} = \qp^W_b\;. \label{eq:pauli-inversion-0}
  1161	\end{align}
  1162	
  1163	Since we only consider finite fields $\F_q$ such that $q = 2^k$ the maximally
  1164	entangled state $\ket{\EPR_q}$ and the corresponding qudit Pauli
  1165	observables/projectors are isomorphic to a tensor product of maximally entangled
  1166	states $\ket{\EPR_2}$ and \emph{qubit} Pauli observables/projectors
  1167	respectively; this is shown in the next lemma.
  1168	This is used to argue that the Pauli basis test (described in
  1169	Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier}) gives a self-test for Pauli observables and
  1170	maximally entangled states over qubits.
  1171	
  1172	\begin{lemma}
  1173	  \label{lem:pauli-binary}
  1174	  For all admissible field sizes $q = 2^k$ and integers $L$, there exists
  1175	  an isomorphism $\phi: (\C^q)^{\otimes L} \to (\C^2)^{\otimes L k}$
  1176	  such that\footnote{ Here we have applied the natural identifications between
  1177	  $(\C^q)^{\ot L} \ot (\C^q)^{\ot L}$ and $(\C^q \ot \C^q)^{\ot L}$,
  1178	  and between $(\C^2)^{\ot L k} \ot (C^2)^{\ot Lk}$ and $(\C^2 \ot
  1179	  \C^2)^{\ot Lk}$.}
  1180	\begin{equation}
  1181	    \label{eq:epr-q-to-epr-2}
  1182	    \phi \otimes \phi \, \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes L} =
  1183	    \ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes L k}\;.
  1184	  \end{equation}

15:The classical low individual degree game is a two-player game based on the low individual degree variant of the multilinearity test of Babai, Fortnow, and Lund. In the basic version, one player (the ``points player'') receives a uniformly random point $u \in \F_q^m$ and answers with a value $a \in \F_q$, while the other player (the ``lines player'') receives a random line through $u$ --- either axis-parallel or diagonal --- and answers with a univariate polynomial describing the restriction of a global function to that line. If the players share a polynomial $g\colon \F_q^m \to \F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$ and answer with $g(u)$ and with the restriction $g|_\ell$, they win with probability $1$; the soundness theorem below states that the converse approximately holds. In the simultaneous version, the players' answers are $k$-tuples, checked coordinatewise against a $k$-tuple of low individual degree polynomials.

   205	We recall the Magic Square game of Mermin and Peres. It is a simple self-test for two EPR pairs, and it allows one to test that a pair of binary observables \emph{anticommutes}; both properties are used in the Pauli basis test. Here it is presented as a binary constraint satisfaction game. Throughout this section and the next, $\sigma^X$ and $\sigma^Z$ denote the single-qubit Pauli observables, with associated two-outcome projective measurements $\{\sigma^W_b\}_{b \in \F_2}$ for $W \in \{X,Z\}$.
   206	
   207	\begin{definition}[The Magic Square game]\label{def:ms-game}
   208		\uses{def:game, def:graph-distribution}
   209		The Magic Square game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{MS}}$ is the following two-player game. There are $9$ variables $x_1,\ldots,x_9$ taking values in $\F_2$, arranged in a $3 \times 3$ grid: the cell in row $r$ and column $c$ contains the variable $x_{3(r-1)+c}$. There are $6$ linear equations over these variables: for each of the three rows and each of the first two columns, the sum of the three variables in it equals $0$; for the third column, the sum of the three variables in it equals $1$.
   210	
   211		The question types are
   212		\begin{align*}
   213			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}} &= \{\mathsf{Constraint}_i : i = 1,2,\ldots,6\}\;,\\
   214			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}} &= \{\mathsf{Variable}_j : j = 1,2,\ldots,9\}\;,\\
   215			\mathcal T^{\mathrm{ms}} &= \mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}} \cup \mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}}\;,
   216		\end{align*}
   217		where $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ for $i \in \{1,2,3\}$ denotes the constraint of row $i$ (with variables $x_{3(i-1)+1}, x_{3(i-1)+2}, x_{3(i-1)+3}$), $\mathsf{Constraint}_4$ and $\mathsf{Constraint}_5$ denote the constraints of the first two columns, and $\mathsf{Constraint}_6$ denotes the constraint of the third column (with variables $x_{i-3}, x_{i}, x_{i+3}$ for $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$, $i \in \{4,5,6\}$).
   218	
   219		The question distribution is as follows: the verifier samples $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ uniformly from $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}}$, then samples $\mathsf{Variable}_j$ uniformly among the three variables appearing in the row or column of $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$; one player, chosen uniformly at random, receives $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ and the other receives $\mathsf{Variable}_j$. Equivalently, the verifier samples a uniformly random edge of the bipartite \emph{type graph} $G^{\mathrm{ms}}$ on vertex sets $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}}$ and $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}}$, whose edges are $\mathsf{Constraint}_i \,\text{---}\, \mathsf{Variable}_{3(i-1)+j}$ for $i,j \in \{1,2,3\}$ and $\mathsf{Constraint}_i \,\text{---}\, \mathsf{Variable}_{(i-3)+3(j-1)}$ for $i \in \{4,5,6\}$, $j \in \{1,2,3\}$ ($18$ edges in total, and no self-loops), and sends one endpoint to a uniformly random player and the other endpoint to the other player.
   220	
   221		The $\mathsf{Constraint}$ player answers with three bits $(\beta_{v_1}, \beta_{v_2}, \beta_{v_3}) \in \F_2^3$, where $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ are the indices of the three variables of $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$; the $\mathsf{Variable}$ player answers with a single bit $\gamma \in \F_2$. The players win if and only if the $\mathsf{Constraint}$ player's answer satisfies the equation associated with $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ and $\gamma = \beta_j$.
   222	\end{definition}

   356	\begin{definition}[Win predicate of the Pauli basis test]\label{def:pauli-win-predicate}
   357		\uses{def:pauli-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ms-game, def:indicator-vector, def:admissible}

   359		% The paper's format table writes the line contents loosely as (u_W, s) and (u_W, s, v);

   367			\item $(\mathsf{Pair},W)$: content $\omega$ as above; answer an element of $\F_2$.
   368			\item $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$: content $\omega$ as above; answer $(\alpha_{v_1}, \alpha_{v_2}, \alpha_{v_3}) \in \F_2^3$, indexed by the variable indices $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ of $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$.
   369			\item $\mathsf{Variable}_j$: content $\omega$ as above; answer an element of $\F_2$.
   370			\item $(\mathsf{Pauli},W)$: content $0$; answer an element of $\F_q^M$.
   371		\end{itemize}
   372		The win predicate $D^{\mathrm{pauli}} = D^{\mathrm{pauli}}_{\mathsf{qldparams}}$ is the function of the tuple $(t_{\mathrm A}, x_{\mathrm A}, t_{\mathrm B}, x_{\mathrm B}, a_{\mathrm A}, a_{\mathrm B})$ determined by the following clauses, evaluated for $w \in \{\mathrm A, \mathrm B\}$ and $W \in \{X,Z\}$; in all cases where no action is indicated, the predicate accepts. In the last four clauses, the content of the player whose type lies in $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{ms}} \cup \{\mathsf{Pair}, (\mathsf{Pair},X), (\mathsf{Pair},Z)\}$ is a tuple $(u_X, u_Z, r_X, r_Z)$, from which the predicate first computes
   373		\begin{equation}
   374			\label{eq:gamma-value}
   375			\gamma = \tr\bigl( (\mathrm{ind}_m(u_X) \cdot r_X) \cdot (\mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \bigr) \in \F_2\;,
   376		\end{equation}

   378		\begin{enumerate}
   379			\item (\textbf{Consistency check}) If $t_{\mathrm A} = t_{\mathrm B}$, accept if and only if $a_{\mathrm A} = a_{\mathrm B}$.

   382				\item If $t_w = (\mathsf{Point},W)$ and $t_{\overline w} = (\mathsf{ALine},W)$, accept if $D^{\mathrm{ld}}_{\mathsf{ldparams}}$ accepts $(\mathsf{Point}, x_w, \mathsf{ALine}, x_{\overline w}, a_w, a_{\overline w})$.

   384			\end{enumerate}
   385			\item (\textbf{Consistency check}) If $t_w = (\mathsf{Point},W)$ and $t_{\overline w} = (\mathsf{Pauli},W)$, accept if $g_{a_{\overline w}}(x_w) = a_w$, where $g_{a_{\overline w}}$ is the low-degree encoding of $a_{\overline w} \in \F_q^M$ (Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}).

60	\begin{remark}
    61	  Unless specified otherwise, all strategies considered in this paper are tensor
    62	  product strategies, and we simply call them \emph{strategies}.
    63	  Similarly, we refer to $\val^*(\game)$ as the \emph{value} of the game
    64	  $\game$.
    65	\end{remark}
    66	
    67	
    68	\begin{definition}[Projective strategies]
    69	  \label{def:projective-strategy}
    70	  We say that a strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ is \emph{projective} if
    71	  all the measurements $\{A^x_a\}_a$ and $\{B^y_b\}_b$ are projective.
    72	\end{definition}
    73	
    74	\begin{definition}\label{rem:symmetric-games}
    75		A game $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ is
    76	  \emph{symmetric} if the question and answer alphabets are the same for both
    77	  players (i.e.\
    78	  $\cal{X} = \cal{Y}$ and $\cal{A} = \cal{B}$), the distribution $\mu$ is
    79	  symmetric (i.e.\
    80	  $\mu(x,y) = \mu(y,x)$), and the decision predicate $D$ treats both players
    81	  symmetrically (i.e.\ for all $x,y,a,b$, $D(x,y,a,b) = D(y,x,b,a)$).
    82	 
    83	We call a strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$
    84	  \emph{symmetric} if $\ket{\psi}$ is a (pure) state in $\mH \otimes \mH$, for some
    85	  Hilbert space $\mH$, that is invariant under permutation of the two factors,
    86	  and the measurement operators of both players are identical.
    87	\end{definition}
    88	
    89	We often specify symmetric games $\game$ and symmetric strategies $\strategy$ using
    90	  a compact notation: we write $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{A}, \mu, D)$ and
    91	  $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, M)$ where $M$ denotes the set of measurement
    92	  operators for both players.
    93	
    94	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:symmetric-strat}
    95	  Let $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{A},  \mu, D)$ be a symmetric game
    96	  such that $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$ for some $\eps\geq 0$.
    97	  Then there exists a symmetric and projective strategy
    98	  $\strategy=(\ket{\psi},M)$ such that $\val^*(\game,\strategy)\geq 1-\eps$.
    99	\end{lemma}
   100	
   101	\begin{proof}
   102	  By definition for any $\eps'>\eps$ there exists a strategy $\strategy'= (\ket{\psi'},A,B)$ such
   103	  that $\val^*(\game,\strategy')\geq 1-\eps'$.
   104	Using Naimark's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark}) we can assume
   105	without loss of generality that $\ket{\psi'}\in\C_{\alice'}^d\otimes \C_{\bob'}^d$ for some integer $d$
   106	  and that for every $x$, $A^x$ and $B^x$ are projective measurements.
   107	Let
   108	  \[
   109	    \ket{\psi} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \big( \ket{0}_\alice \ket{1}_\bob
   110	    \ket{\psi'}_{\alice'\bob'} + \ket{1}_\alice \ket{0}_\bob
   111	    \ket{\psi'_\tau}_{\alice'\bob'}\big) \in (\C_{\alice}^2 \otimes
   112	    \C_{\alice'}^d) \otimes (\C_\bob^2 \otimes \C_{\bob'}^d)\;,
   113	  \]
   114	  where $\ket{\psi'_\tau}$ is obtained from $\ket{\psi}$ by permuting the two
   115	  players' registers.
   116	  Observe that $\ket{\psi}$ is invariant under permutation of $\alice\alice'$
   117	  and $\bob\bob'$.
   118	
   119	  For any question $x\in \cal{X}$ define the measurement $M^x = \{M^x_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$
   120	  acting on the Hilbert space $\C^2 \otimes \C^d$ as follows:
   121	  \[
   122	  	M^x_a = \ketbra{0}{0} \otimes A^x_a + \ketbra{1}{1} \otimes B^x_a \;,
   123	  \]
   124		i.e.\ for $\ket{\varphi} \in \C^d$, $M^x_a(\ket{0}\ket{\varphi})=\ket{0}A^x_a\ket{\varphi}$ and $M^x_a(\ket{1}\ket{\varphi})=\ket{1}B^x_a\ket{\varphi}$.
   125	  When Alice receives question $x$, she measures $M^x$ on registers $\alice \alice'$, and when Bob receives 
   126	  question $y$, he measures $M^y$ on registers $\bob \bob'$.
   127	Using that by assumption the decision predicate $D$ for $\game$ is symmetric,
   128	  it is not hard to verify that $\val^*(\game,\strategy) =
   129	  \val^*(\game,\strategy')$.
   130	\end{proof}
   131	
   132	\begin{definition}
   133	  \label{def:comm-strategy}
   134	  Let $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ be a game, and let
   135	  $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ be a strategy for $\game$ such that  $\mH_A = \mH_B$.
   136	  Let $S \subseteq \cal{X} \times \cal{Y}$ denote the support of the question
   137	  distribution $\mu$, i.e.\ the set of $(x,y)$ such that $\mu(x,y)>0$.
   138	  We say that $\strategy$ is a \emph{commuting strategy for $\game$} if for all
   139	  question pairs $(x, y) \in S$, we have $[A^x_a, B^y_b] = 0$ 
   140	  for all $a
   141	  \in \cal{A}, b \in \cal{B}$, where $[A, B] = AB - BA$ denotes the commutator.
   142	\end{definition}
   143	
   144	\begin{definition}[Consistent measurements]
   145	  \label{def:consistent-measurement}
   146	  Let $\cal{A}$ be a finite set, let $\ket{\psi} \in \mH \otimes \mH$ be a
   147	  state, and let $\{ M_a \}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ be a projective measurement on
   148	  $\mH$.
   149	  We say that \emph{$\{M_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$} if
   150	  and only if
   151	  \begin{equation*}
   152	    \forall a \in \mA\;,\quad M_a \otimes \Id_\bob\, \ket{\psi}
   153	    = \Id_\alice \otimes M_a\, \ket{\psi}\;.
   154	  \end{equation*}
   155		When the state $\ket{\psi}$ is clear from context we simply say that \emph{$\{M_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is consistent}.
   156	\end{definition}
   157	
   158	The terminology ``consistent'' arises from the fact that when the measurement $\{M_a\}$ is performed on both registers of $\ket{\psi}$, the probability of obtaining twice the same outcome is 
   159	\[ \sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \otimes M_a \ket{\psi}\,=\, \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Id_\alice \otimes (M_a)^2 \ket{\psi} \,=\, \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Id_\alice \otimes M_a \ket{\psi} \,=\,1\;,\]
   160	where the first equality is by definition of consistency, the second uses that $\{M_a\}$ is projective, and the last uses $\sum_a M_a=\Id$. 
   161	
   162	\begin{definition}[Consistent strategies]
   163	  \label{def:consistent-strategy}
   164		Let $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ be a projective strategy with state
   165	  $\ket{\psi} \in \mH \otimes \mH$, for some Hilbert space~$\mH$, which is
   166	  defined on question alphabets $\cal{X}$ and~$\cal{Y}$ and answer alphabets
   167	  $\cal{A}$ and~$\cal{B}$, respectively.
   168	  We say that the strategy $\strategy$ is \emph{consistent} if for all $x \in
   169	  \cal{X}$, the measurement $\{A^x_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is consistent on
   170	  $\ket{\psi}$ and if for all $y \in \cal{Y}$, the measurement $\{B^y_b\}_{b \in
   171	    \cal{B}}$ is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$.
   172	\end{definition}
   173	
   174	We almost always restrict our attention to symmetric strategies. In this case, consistency implies that whenever both players are sent the same question, they provide the same answer. 
   175	
   176	\begin{definition}
   177	  \label{def:spcc}
   178	  We say that a strategy $\strategy$ for a game $\game$ is \emph{PCC} if it is projective, consistent, and commuting for $\game$.
   179	  Additionally, we say that a PCC strategy $\strategy$ is \emph{SPCC} if it is furthermore symmetric.
   180	\end{definition}
   181	
   182	
   183	Recall that for a (pure) state $\ket{\psi}\in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$, the \emph{Schmidt rank} of $\ket{\psi}$ is the smallest integer $k$ such that 
   184	\[ \ket{\psi} = \sum_{i=1}^k\, \alpha_i \ket{u_i}\otimes \ket{v_i}\;,\]
   185	for some orthonormal families $\{\ket{u_i}\}\subset \mH_\alice$ and $\{\ket{v_i}\}\subset\mH_\bob$ and $\alpha_i>0$. The coefficients $\alpha_i$ are uniquely defined by $\ket{\psi}$ and called \emph{Schmidt coefficients}. The state $\ket{\psi}$ is called \emph{maximally entangled} if $\alpha_i=\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}$ for all $i=1,\ldots,k$.  
   186	
   187	
   188	\begin{definition}[Entanglement requirements of a game]
   189	  \label{def:ent}
   190		For all games $\game$ and $\nu \in [0, 1]$, let $\Ent(\game, \nu)$ denote the
   210	  maximally entangled state.
   211	  (The equivalence is extended to infinite-dimensional strategies, as well as
   212	  correlations induced by limits of finite-dimensional strategies,
   213	  in~\cite{kim2018synchronous}.)

   215	\subsection{Distance measures}
   216	
   217	We introduce several distance measures that are used throughout.
   218	
   219	\begin{definition}[Distance between states]
   220	  \label{def:state-distance}
   221	
   222		Let $\{\ket{\psi_n}\}_{n\in \N}$ and $\{\ket{\psi'_n}\}_{n\in \N}$ be two
   223	  families of states in the same space $\mH$.
   224	  For some function $\delta : \N \to [0,1]$ we say that $\{ \ket{\psi_n} \}$ and
   225	  $\{ \ket{\psi'_n} \}$ are \emph{$\delta$-close}, denoted as $\ket{\psi}
   226	  \approx_\delta \ket{\psi'}$, if $ \norm{\ket{\psi_n} - \ket{\psi'_n}}^2 =
   227	  O(\delta(n))$.
   228	  (For convenience we generally leave the dependence of the states and $\delta$
   229	  on the indexing parameter $n$ implicit, writing e.g.\ $\ket{\psi}$ for $\ket{\psi_n}$.)
   230	\end{definition}
   231	
   232	\begin{definition}[Consistency between POVMs]
   233	  \label{def:consistency}
   234		Let $\mX$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mX$.
   235	  Let $\ket{\psi} \in \cal{H}_A \otimes \cal{H}_B$ be a quantum state, and for
   236	  all $x\in \mX$, $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ POVMs.
   237	  We write
   238	  \begin{equation*}
   239	    A^x_a \otimes I_\bob \simeq_\delta I_\alice \otimes B^x_a
   240	  \end{equation*}
   241	  on state $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ if
   242	  \begin{equation*}
   243	    \E_{x\sim \mu} \sum_{a\ne b} \bra{\psi} A^x_a \otimes B^x_b \ket{\psi}
   244	    = O(\delta)\;.\footnote{Here the use of the $O(\cdot)$ notation refers to the fact that the notation will often be used to measure consistency for \emph{famillies} of POVM and states indexed by an implicit parameter $n\in \mathbb{N}$, which will always be clear from context but omitted for legibility, see Definition~\ref{def:state-distance}. The $O(\cdot)$ is taken as $n\to\infty$.}
   245	  \end{equation*}
   246	  In this case, we say that $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ are
   247	  \emph{$\delta$-consistent} on $\ket{\psi}$.
   248	\end{definition}
   249	
   250	Note that a consistent measurement on $\ket{\psi}$ according to
   251	Definition~\ref{def:consistent-measurement} is $0$-consistent with itself on the same $\ket{\psi}$ and under
   252	the singleton distribution, according to Definition~\ref{def:consistency} (and
   253	vice-versa). This is because 
   254	\[ \sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \otimes M_a \ket{\psi} =1 \,\implies \, \forall a\;,\;\Id\otimes M_a \ket{\psi} = M_a \otimes \Id \ket{\psi}\;,\]
   255	because using that $\{M_a\}$ is a POVM there must be equality in the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
   256	\[ 1 = \sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \otimes M_a \ket{\psi}\, \leq\, \Big(\sum_a \|\Id\otimes M_a \ket{\psi}\|^2 \Big)\Big(\sum_a \|M_a\otimes \Id \ket{\psi}\|^2 \Big)^{1/2} \,\leq\,1 \;.\]
   257	
   258	\begin{definition}[Distance between POVMs]
   259	  \label{def:povm-distance}
   260		Let $\mX$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mX$. 
   261	  Let $\ket{\psi} \in \cal{H}$ be a quantum state, and for all $x\in \mX$,
   262	  $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ two POVMs on $\mH$.
   263	  We say that \emph{$\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ are $\delta$-close on state
   264	    $\ket{\psi}$ and under distribution $\mu$} if
   265	  \begin{equation*}
   266	    \E_{x\sim \mu} \sum_a \norm{ (M^x_a - N^x_a) \ket{\psi} }^2 \leq O(\delta)\;,
   267	  \end{equation*}
   268	  and we write $M^x_a \approx_\delta N^x_a$ to denote this when the state
   269	  $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ are clear from context.
   270	  This distance is referred to as the \emph{state-dependent} distance.
   271	\end{definition}
   272	
   273	\begin{definition}[Distance between strategies]
   274	  \label{def:strategy-distance}
   275	  Let $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ be a nonlocal game
   276	  and let $\strategy = (\psi, A, B)$, $\strategy' = (\psi', A', B')$ be 
   277	  strategies for $\game$.
   278	  For $\delta\in[0,1]$ we say that \emph{$\strategy$ is $\delta$-close to
   279	    $\strategy'$} if the following conditions hold.
   280	  \begin{enumerate}
   281		\item The states $\ket{\psi}, \ket{\psi'}$ are states in the same
   282	    Hilbert space $\mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ and are $\delta$-close.
   283		\item For all $x \in \cal{X}, y \in \cal{Y}$, we have $A^x_a \approx_\delta
   284	    (A')^x_a$ and $B^y_b \approx_\delta (B')^y_b$, with the approximations
   285	    holding under the distribution $\mu$, and on either $\ket{\psi}$ or
   286	    $\ket{\psi'}$.
   287	  \end{enumerate}
   288	\end{definition}
   289

   291	state-dependent distance without proof.

   293	discussion and proofs.

   465	The following lemma is a slightly modified version of~\cite[Fact~4.34]{NW19}.
   466	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:ld-sandwich}
   467	  Let $k \geq 0$ be an integer and let $\eps>0$.
   468	  Let $\mX$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution over $\mX$.
   469	  For each $1 \leq i \leq k$ let $\mG_i$ be a finite set of functions $g_i : \mY
   470	  \rightarrow \mR_i$ and for each $x \in \mX$ let $\{G^{i,\, x}_g\}_{g\in
   471	    \mG_i}$ be a projective measurement.
   472	  Suppose that for all $i\in \{1,\ldots,k\}$, $\mG_i$ satisfies the following
   473	  property: for any two $g_i \neq g_i' \in \mG_i$, the probability that $g_i(y)
   474	  = g_i'(y)$ over a uniformly random $y \in \mY$ is at most $\eps$.
   475	
   476	  Let $\bigl\{ A^{x}_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_k} \bigr\}$ be a projective
   477	  measurement with outcomes $(g_1,\ldots,g_k) \in \mG_1\times\cdots\times
   478	  \mG_k$.
   479	  For each $1 \leq i \leq k$, suppose that on average over $x \sim \mu$ and
   480	  $y\in \mY$ sampled uniformly at random,
   481	  \begin{equation}\label{eq:ld-sandwich-1}
   482	    A^{x}_{[\eval_y(\cdot)_i = a_i]} \abc G^{i,\, x}_{[\eval_y(\cdot)=a_i]}\;.
   483	  \end{equation}
   484	  Define the POVM family $\{C^x_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_k}\}$, for $x\in \mX$, by
   485	  \begin{equation*}
   486	    C^x_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_k} = G^{k,\, x}_{g_1} \cdots
   487	    G^{2,\, x}_{g_{k-1}} \, G^{1,\, x}_{g_k} \, G^{2,\, x}_{g_{k-1}} \cdots
   488	    G^{k,\, x}_{g_1}\;.
   489	  \end{equation*}
   490	  Then on average over $x\sim \mu$ and $y\in \mY$ sampled uniformly at random,
   491	  \begin{equation}\label{eq:ld-sandwich-2}
   492	    A^x_{[\eval_y(\cdot) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots,\, a_k)]} \abc[k(\delta+\eps)^{1/2}]
   493	    C^x_{[\eval_y(\cdot) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots,\, a_k)]}\;.
   494	\end{equation}
   495	\end{lemma}

   499	  only modification needed to insert the dependence on $x$ for all measurements

    57	\begin{definition}[Typed conditionally linear functions]
    58	  Let $\type$ be a finite set and $V$ be $\F^n$ for some integer $n \geq 0$.
    59	  A \emph{$\type$-typed family of $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions}
    60	  (implicitly, \emph{on $V$}) is a collection $\{L_\tvar\}_{\tvar \in \type}$
    61	  such that, for each $\tvar \in \type$, $L_\tvar$ is an $\ell$-level
    62	  conditionally linear function on~$V$.
    63	\end{definition}

    65	\begin{definition}[Graph distribution]
    66	  \label{def:graph-distribution}
    67	  Let $G = (U, E)$ be an undirected graph with vertex set $U$ and edge set~$E$.
    68	  Edges in~$E$ are written as multisets $\{u, v\}$ of two vertices; the case $u
    69	  = v$ represents a self-loop.
    70	  Suppose there are $m$ edges, $k$ of which are self-loops.
    71	  Then the \emph{graph distribution $\mu_G$ of~$G$} is the distribution over
    72	  $U\times U$ such that for every $(u, v)\in U\times U$,
    73	  \begin{equation*}
    74	    \mu_G(u, v) =
    75	    \begin{cases}
    76	      1/(2m-k) & \text{if $\{u, v\} \in E$},\\
    77	      0 & \text{otherwise}.
    78	    \end{cases}
    79	  \end{equation*}
    80	  This is identical to the uniform distribution over pairs $(u, v)\in U\times U$
    81	  such that $\{u, v\} \in E$.
    82	\end{definition}

    86	  $L=\{L_\lvar\}_{\lvar\in\type},R=\{R_\rvar\}_{\rvar\in\type}$ be $\type$-typed
    87	  families of conditionally linear functions on~$V$.
    88	  Let $G = (\type, E)$ be a graph with vertex set $\type$.
    89	  The \emph{$(\type, G)$-typed conditionally linear distribution $\mu_{L,\,
    90	      R}^G$ corresponding to~$(L, R)$} is the distribution over pairs $( (\lvar,
    91	  x), (\rvar, y) )$, where $(\lvar, \rvar)$ is drawn from $\mu_G$ and $(x,y)$ is
    92	  drawn from $\mu_{L_\lvar,\, R_\rvar}$.
    93	\end{definition}

   255	    \label{eq:cl-last-ell}
   256	    L_{\leq k}(x)
   257	    & = v + L'_{v,\, <k} (x^{V_{>1}}) \\
   258	    & = v + \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} x^{L'_{v,\, i}}
   259	    = \sum_{i = 1}^{k} x^{L_{i}}, \label{eq:cl-last-ell2}
   260	  \end{align}
   261	  where $L'_{v,\, i}$ is the $i$-th linear map of $L_{>1,\, v}$ with prefix
   262	  $L'_{v,\, <i}(x)$ and $L_i$ is the $i$-th linear map of $L$ with prefix
   263	  $L_{<i}(x)$.
   264	  The second equality follows from the inductive hypothesis applied to $L'_{v,\,
   265	    <k}$ and the third equality follows from the definition of $L_{i}$.
   266	  Line~\eqref{eq:cl-last-ell2} implies \cref{enu:cl-map-sum} of the lemma.
   267	  
   268	  Finally, \Cref{enu:cl-last-ell} follows from~\eqref{eq:cl-last-ell} where we
   269	  set $k = \ell$ and observe that $L'_{x^{L_1},\, \le \ell-1}$ is equal to
   270	  $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ by the inductive hypothesis.
   271	  This shows that $L_{\le k}$, $V_{k,\, u}$, and $L_{k,\, u}$ satisfy the
   272	  conditions of the lemma and completes the induction.
   273	\end{proof}
   274	
   275	We note that the marginal functions, factor spaces, and linear maps of a given
   276	CL function $L$ may not be unique; for example, consider the identity function
   277	on a linear space $V = \F^n$.
   278	This is clearly a $1$-level CL function, but it can also be viewed as a
   279	$k$-level CL function for $k \in \{2, \ldots, n\}$ with an arbitrary partition
   280	of $V$ into factor spaces.
   281	
   282	\begin{lemma}
   283	  \label{lem:cl-concat}
   284	  Let $\ell, k \ge 0$ be integers and $U = \F^n$, $V = \F^m$ be linear spaces.
   285	  Suppose $L$ is a $k$-level CL function on $U$ and $R_u$ is an $\ell$-level CL
   286	  function on $V$ for each $u \in L(U)$.
   287	  Then the \emph{concatenation} $T$ of $L$ and $\{R_u\}_u$ defined as
   288	  \begin{equation*}
   289	    T (x) = L(x^U) + R_{L(x^U)} (x^V)
   290	  \end{equation*}
   291	  is a $(k+\ell)$-level conditionally linear function on $U\oplus V$.
   292	\end{lemma}
   293	
   294	\begin{proof}
   295	  We prove the claim by induction on $k$.
   296	  The case $k = 0$ follows from the Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}.
   297	  Assume that the lemma holds for $L$ being at most $(k-1)$-level.
   298	  By Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}, there are complementary register subspaces
   299	  $U_1$ and $U_{>1}$ of $U$, a linear function $L_1$ on $U_1$, and a family of
   300	  $(k-1)$-level CL functions $L_{>1,\, v}$ for $v \in L_1(U_1)$ such that
   301	  \begin{equation*}
   302	    L(x^U) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}}).
   303	  \end{equation*}
   304	  For all $x^{L_1}$, define the function $T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ on $U_{>1} \oplus V$ as
   305	  \begin{equation*}
   306	    T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1} \oplus V}) = L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}}) +
   307	    R_{x^{L_1} + x^{L_{>1}}}(x^V),
   308	  \end{equation*}
   309	  the concatenation of $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ and $\{ R_{L(x^U)} \}_{x^{L_{>1}}}$
   310	  where $L_{>1}$ is the shorthand notation of $L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$.
   311	  By the induction hypothesis, $T_{>1,\, x^{L_1}}$ is $(k+\ell-1)$-level
   312	  conditionally linear.
   313	  The lemma follows from Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}.
   314	\end{proof}
   315	\begin{lemma}[Direct sums of CL functions]
   316	  \label{lem:cl-func-prod}
   317	  Let $V^{(1)}, V^{(2)}, \ldots, V^{(m)}$ be register subspaces of $V$ such that
   318	  $V = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$.
   319	  Suppose that, for each $j\in\{1, 2, \ldots, m\}$, $L^{(j)}$ is an
   320	  $\ell_j$-level conditionally linear function on $V^{(j)}$.
   321	  Then the direct sum $L = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}$ is an $\ell$-level CL
   322	  function over $V$ for $\ell = \max_j \{\ell_j\}$, where $L$ is defined by
   323	  \begin{equation*}
   324	    L(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m  L^{(j)}(x^{(j)})
   325	  \end{equation*}
   326	  for all $x = \sum_{j=1}^m x^{(j)} \in \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$.
   327	\end{lemma}
   328	
   329	\begin{proof}
   330	  It is easy to see that an $\ell$-level CL function is also $k$-level
   331	  conditionally linear for all $k \ge \ell$.
   332	  Hence, it suffices to prove the claim where $\ell_j = \ell$ for $j=1, 2,
   333	  \ldots, m$.
   334	
   335	  We prove the theorem by an induction on $\ell$.
   336	  For $\ell = 1$, the functions $L^{(j)}$ are linear and the claim follows by
   337	  the fact that the direct sum of linear maps is linear.
   338	
   339	  Assume now the theorem holds for conditionally linear functions of level at
   340	  most $\ell-1$ and $L^{(j)}$ are $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions
   341	  for $j=1, 2, ,\ldots, m$.
   342	  By definition, $L^{(j)}$ is the concatenation of conditionally linear
   343	  functions $L^{(j)}_{1}$ on $V^{(j)}_1$ and $\{ L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j} \}_{v_j}$
   344	  on $V^{(j)}_{>1}$ of levels $1$, and $\ell-1$ respectively.
   345	  Furthermore,
   346	  \begin{equation*}
   347	    L(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)} (x^{(j)}) = \sum_{j=1}^m \Bigl( v_j +
   348	    L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j}
   349	    \Bigl((x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_{>1}} \Bigr) \Bigr),
   350	  \end{equation*}
   351	  where $v_j = L^{(j)}_{1}\Bigl( (x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_1}
   352	    \Bigr)$.
   353	  By the induction hypothesis,
   354	  \begin{equation*}
   355	    L_{1} (x^{V_1}) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}_{1}\Bigl( (x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_1}
   356	    \Bigr),\quad L_{>1,\, v} (x^{V_{>1}}) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}_{>1,\, v_j}
   357	    \Bigl((x^{(j)})^{V^{(j)}_{>1}} \Bigr)
   358	  \end{equation*}
   359	  are $1$-level and $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear respectively for $v =
   360	  \sum_j v_j$, $V_1 = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}_1$, and $V_{>1} =
   361	  \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}_{>1}$.
   362	  This proves that $L$ is $\ell$-level conditionally linear.
   363	\end{proof}

   365	\begin{lemma}
   366	  \label{lem:cl-dist-prod}
   367	  For each $i \in \{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $L^{(i)}, R^{(i)} : V^{(i)} \to V^{(i)}$
   368	  be $\ell_i$-level conditionally linear functions and let $L, R: V \to V$ be the
   369	  direct sums $L = \bigoplus_i L_i$ and $R = \bigoplus_i R_i$, respectively, as
   370	  defined in Lemma~\ref{lem:cl-func-prod}.
   371	  Then the conditionally linear distribution $\mu_{L, R}$ is the product
   372	  distribution $\prod_{i=1}^m \mu_{L^{(i)},\, R^{(i)}}$ over $V \times V$.
   373	\end{lemma}
   374	
   375	\begin{proof}
   376		The distribution $\mu_{L,R}$ is the distribution over pairs $(L(x),R(x))$
   377	  where $x$ is sampled uniformly from $V \times V$.
   378	  By Lemma~\ref{lem:cl-func-prod}, this is equivalent to the distribution over
   379	  pairs $\bigl( (L_i(x^{V_i}))_{i=1}^m, (R_i(x^{V_i}))_{i=1}^m \bigr)$ where $x$
   380	  is chosen uniformly at random from $V$.
   381	  This distribution is exactly the product of the distributions $
   382	  \mu_{L^{(i)},\, R^{(i)}}$ for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, m$.
   383	\end{proof}

515		Let $L, R \colon V \to V$ be conditionally linear functions. The \emph{conditionally linear distribution $\mu_{L,R}$ corresponding to $(L,R)$} is the distribution over pairs $(L(x), R(x)) \in V \times V$ for $x$ drawn uniformly at random from $V$.
   516	\end{definition}
   517	
   518	Note that both players' questions are generated from the \emph{same} uniformly random seed $x$; this shared-seed structure is what the introspection technique exploits. The following lemma elucidates the structural properties of $\ell$-level CL functions. Recall that $x^{L_{<k}}$ and $x^{L_k}$ denote $L_{<k}(x)$ and $L_{k,\,u}(x^{V_{k,\,u}})$ where $u = L_{<k}(x)$.

   520	\begin{lemma}[Structure of conditionally linear functions]\label{lem:cl-kth}
   521		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.CLData, MIPStarRE.QPBT.isCondLinear_iff_nonempty_clData}
   522		\leanok
   523		\uses{def:cl-func, def:register-subspace}
   524		Let $\ell \ge 1$ and $V = \F^n$ for some integer $n \ge 0$. A function $L \colon V \to V$ is an $\ell$-level CL function if and only if the following collection of functions and subspaces exists:
   525		\begin{enumerate}
   526			\item[(i)] for each $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$, a function $L_{\le k} \colon V \to V$, called the \emph{$k$-th marginal of $L$};
   527			\item[(ii)] for each $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$ and $u \in L_{<k}(V)$, a register subspace $V_{k,\,u}$ of $V$, called the \emph{$k$-th factor space with prefix $u$};
   528			\item[(iii)] for each $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$ and $u \in L_{<k}(V)$, a linear map $L_{k,\,u} \colon V_{k,\,u} \to V_{k,\,u}$, called the \emph{$k$-th linear map of $L$ with prefix $u$};
   529		\end{enumerate}
   530		such that the following conditions hold for all $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$:
   531		\begin{enumerate}
   532			\item $L_{\le k}$ is a $k$-level CL function on $V$;
   533			\item $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^{\ell} V_{i,\,x^{L_{<i}}}$ for all $x \in V$;
   534			\item $L_{\le k}(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} x^{L_i}$ for all $x \in V$, where $L_i$ is shorthand notation for $L_{i,\,x^{L_{<i}}}$;
   535			\item $L = L_{\le \ell}$.
   536		\end{enumerate}
   537		As in condition 3, we sometimes use $V_k$ and $L_k$ to denote $V_{k,\,u}$ and $L_{k,\,u}$ respectively, leaving the prefix $u$ implicit.
   538		Index the decomposition levels by $0,\ldots,\ell-1$; level $r$ corresponds
   539		to the paper's level $r+1$.
   540	\end{lemma}
   541	\begin{proof}
   542		\uses{def:cl-func}
   543		For the ``if'' direction, conditions 1 and 4 immediately exhibit $L$ as an $\ell$-level CL function. For the ``only if'' direction one constructs the marginals, factor spaces, and linear maps by induction on $\ell$. In the base case $\ell = 1$ take $L_{\le 1} = L$, $V_1 = V$, and $L_1 = L$. For the inductive step, write $L(x) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\,x^{L_1}}(x^{V_{>1}})$ as in Definition~\ref{def:cl-func} and apply the inductive hypothesis to each $(\ell-1)$-level function $L_{>1,\,v}$, obtaining its marginals, factor spaces, and linear maps over $V_{>1}$. Define $L_{\le 1} = L_1$ with first factor space $V_1$, and for $k \ge 2$ define $L_{\le k}(x) = x^{L_1} + L'_{x^{L_1},\,<k}(x^{V_{>1}})$, with the $k$-th factor space and linear map of $L$ with prefix $u$ given by those of $L_{>1,\,v}$ at index $k-1$ with prefix $w$, where $v = u^{V_1}$ and $w = u^{V_{>1}}$. Conditions 1--4 are then verified directly from the inductive hypothesis: the direct-sum decomposition of $V_{>1}$ extends to $V$ by adjoining $V_1$, and the sum formula for $L_{\le k}$ follows by unfolding the inductive marginals.
   544	\end{proof}
   545	
   546	The marginal functions, factor spaces, and linear maps of a given CL function $L$ need not be unique. For example, the identity function on $V = \F^n$ is a $1$-level CL function, but it can also be viewed as a $k$-level CL function for any $k \in \{2, \dots, n\}$ with an arbitrary partition of $V$ into factor spaces.

   548	\begin{lemma}[Concatenation of conditionally linear functions]\label{lem:cl-concat}
   549		\uses{def:cl-func}
   550		Let $\ell, k \ge 0$ be integers and let $U = \F^n$, $V = \F^m$ be linear spaces. Suppose $L$ is a $k$-level CL function on $U$ and, for each $u \in L(U)$, $R_u$ is an $\ell$-level CL function on $V$. Then the \emph{concatenation} $T$ of $L$ and $\{R_u\}_u$, defined by
   551		\[
   552			T(x) = L(x^U) + R_{L(x^U)}(x^V)\,,
   553		\]
   554		is a $(k+\ell)$-level conditionally linear function on $U \oplus V$.
   555	\end{lemma}
   556	\begin{proof}
   557		\uses{def:cl-func}
   558		By induction on $k$. The case $k = 0$ follows directly from Definition~\ref{def:cl-func}, since then $L = 0$ and $T$ acts by the single $\ell$-level function $R_0$ on the register subspace $V$. For the inductive step, write $L(x^U) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\,x^{L_1}}(x^{U_{>1}})$ with complementary register subspaces $U_1$ and $U_{>1}$ of $U$.    565	\begin{lemma}[Direct sums of conditionally linear functions]\label{lem:cl-func-prod}

   569		Let $m \ge 1$ be an integer and let $V^{(1)}, V^{(2)}, \dots, V^{(m)}$ be register subspaces of $V$ such that $V = \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$.    570		\[
   571			L(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m L^{(j)}(x^{(j)})
   572		\]
   573		for all $x = \sum_{j=1}^m x^{(j)} \in \bigoplus_{j=1}^m V^{(j)}$, is an $\ell$-level CL function on $V$ for $\ell = \max_j \{\ell_j\}$; the maximum exists since $m \ge 1$.

   575	\begin{proof}
   576		\uses{def:cl-func}
   577		Since an $\ell$-level CL function is also $k$-level conditionally linear for all $k \ge \ell$, it suffices to prove the claim when $\ell_j = \ell$ for all $j$. Proceed by induction on $\ell$. Then the conditionally linear distribution $\mu_{L,R}$ is the product distribution $\prod_{i=1}^m \mu_{L^{(i)},\,R^{(i)}}$ over $V \times V$.

   152	\begin{definition}[Consistent measurements]\label{def:consistent-measurement}
   153		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.Measurement.IsConsistentOn}
   154		\leanok
   155		\uses{def:povm-conventions}
   156		Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite set, let $\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal H \ot \mathcal H$ be a state, and let $\{M_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ be a projective measurement on $\mathcal H$. We say that \emph{$\{M_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$} if and only if
   157		\[
   158			\forall a \in \mathcal A\,, \qquad M_a \ot \Id_B\, \ket{\psi} = \Id_A \ot M_a\, \ket{\psi}\,.
   159		\]
   160		When the state $\ket{\psi}$ is clear from context we simply say that $\{M_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ is consistent.
   161	\end{definition}
   162	
   163	The terminology arises from the fact that when the measurement $\{M_a\}$ is performed on both registers of $\ket{\psi}$, the probability of obtaining twice the same outcome is
   164	\[
   165		\sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \ot M_a \ket{\psi} = \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Id_A \ot (M_a)^2 \ket{\psi} = \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Id_A \ot M_a \ket{\psi} = 1\,,
   166	\]
   167	where the first equality is by the definition of consistency, the second uses that $\{M_a\}$ is projective, and the last uses $\sum_a M_a = \Id$.

Equivalently, the verifier samples a uniformly random edge of the bipartite \emph{type graph} $G^{\mathrm{ms}}$ on vertex sets $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mc}}$ and $\mathcal T^{\mathrm{mv}}$, whose edges are $\mathsf{Constraint}_i \,\text{---}\, \mathsf{Variable}_{3(i-1)+j}$ for $i,j \in \{1,2,3\}$ and $\mathsf{Constraint}_i \,\text{---}\, \mathsf{Variable}_{(i-3)+3(j-1)}$ for $i \in \{4,5,6\}$, $j \in \{1,2,3\}$ ($18$ edges in total, and no self-loops), and sends one endpoint to a uniformly random player and the other endpoint to the other player.
   220	
   221		The $\mathsf{Constraint}$ player answers with three bits $(\beta_{v_1}, \beta_{v_2}, \beta_{v_3}) \in \F_2^3$, where $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ are the indices of the three variables of $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$; the $\mathsf{Variable}$ player answers with a single bit $\gamma \in \F_2$. The players win if and only if the $\mathsf{Constraint}$ player's answer satisfies the equation associated with $\mathsf{Constraint}_i$ and $\gamma = \beta_j$.
   222	\end{definition}

     3	MIPStarRE Lean names and documentation should be written for readers comparing
     4	the formalization with the paper and blueprint.
     5	
     6	This is a project-local supplement to the Mathlib-derived documentation,
     7	naming, and style guides in the lean-conventions skill's `MATHLIB_doc`,
     8	`MATHLIB_naming`, and `MATHLIB_style` references.
     9	
    10	## Scope
    11	
    12	These guidelines apply to:
    13	
    14	- public Lean declaration names and namespace names;
    15	- module docstrings;
    16	- declaration docstrings;
    17	- documentation-visible section comments;
    18	- explanatory comments that describe the mathematical role of a declaration.
    19	- blueprint prose and formalization-support notes;
    20	- issue titles and issue bodies;
    21	- PR titles and PR descriptions.
    22	
    23	## Source of Truth
    24	
    25	Use terminology from the following sources, in this order:
    26	
    27	1. `references/ldt-paper/`
    28	2. `blueprint/src/chapter/`
    29	3. established local conventions in nearby Lean files
    30	
    31	When the paper has a term for the object, use that term. For Section 5, for
    32	example, prefer orthogonalization lemma, truncation function, rounding to
    33	projectors, rank reduction, and completing to measurement.
    34	
    35	## Reference Notation And Terminology
    36	
    37	The notation and terminology of the original reference are the default for
    38	reader-facing mathematical text.  A reader should be able to compare a Lean
    39	docstring, blueprint paragraph, issue, or PR description with the cited source
    40	without first learning a private vocabulary used by the formalization.
    41	
    42	When Lean must use a different name or representation, define the deviation in a
    43	location which future readers can find from the affected statement.  Use the
    44	first applicable location in the following order:
    45	
    46	1. the declaration docstring of the public object whose name or representation
    47	   differs from the paper;
    48	2. the module docstring of the defining Lean file, when the deviation concerns a
    49	   family of declarations in that file;
    50	3. the relevant blueprint paragraph, when the notation appears only in the
    51	   blueprint;
    52	4. a report under `docs/reports/` or `docs/paper-gaps/`, when the deviation is a
    53	   larger discrepancy between the paper, blueprint, and Lean.
    54	
    55	The explanation should say:
    56	
    57	- the notation or term used in the paper;
    58	- the Lean object or name which represents it;
    59	- the mathematical reason for the difference, if there is one;
    60	- the scope in which the replacement should be used.
    61	
    62	A PR description may mention the deviation, but it should not be the only place
    63	where future readers can learn it.
    64	
    65	Formalization-only auxiliary lemmas should be introduced as such.  Their prose
    66	should name the nearby paper equation, theorem, or construction they support,
    67	rather than presenting the auxiliary name as paper terminology.
    68	
    69	## Naming Norm
    70	
    71	Names and prose should describe the mathematical object, hypothesis, or
    72	conclusion. They should not encode the history of how the formalization was
    73	assembled.
    74	
    75	Avoid presenting words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`, `raw`,
    76	`oneShot`, or `liveBlock` as mathematical terminology unless the cited source
    77	uses them with that meaning. Likewise, avoid implementation-local substitutes
    78	such as `projectivization` or `spectral truncation` when the paper gives a
    79	clearer phrase.
    80	
    81	This is a general rule for the repository, not only a rule for file splits.
    82	Module names, namespace names, public declarations, theorem fields, docstrings,
    83	blueprint-facing names, issue titles, and spec documents should name the
    84	mathematical layer under discussion, not the local workflow step, paper line
    85	number, or implementation history.

   117	### Shared helpers
   118	
   119	When the same (or nearly the same) helper declaration appears in two or
   120	more chapter-local leaves, the copies should be consolidated into a single
   121	shared helper in an appropriate common module.  This avoids duplication and
   122	ensures that fixes, generalizations, or upstream replacements apply to all
   123	call sites at once.  Issue [#1145] tracks this work across the repository.
   124	
   125	Procedure:
   126	
   127	1. **Confirm equivalence.**  Compare the statement of each copy.  If the
   128	   types differ only by a chapter-specific parameterization (e.g.,
   129	   `SubMeas (Polynomial params) ι` vs `SubMeas (Point params) ι`),
   130	   parameterize the shared helper over that type via a `variable` or
   131	   explicit argument.
   132	2. **Find the right home.**  Prefer a module that is already imported by
   133	   both call sites.  Typical candidates:
   134	   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Basic/` for parameter-free operators and bounds,
   135	   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Preliminaries/` for polynomial/field/character lemmas,
   136	   - The highest chapter that is a common dependency of the two sites.
   137	3. **Name mathematically.**  Give the shared helper a name that describes
   138	   what it states, not which chapter it originally came from.
   139	4. **Replace call sites.**  Delete the chapter-local copies and replace
   140	   their uses with the shared helper.  A thin wrapper is allowed only when it
   141	   preserves a paper-facing or blueprint-facing name that external readers
   142	   need to search for; such wrappers should have a docstring or compatibility
   143	   comment explaining why the alias exists.  Remove the wrapper once that
   144	   paper-facing name is no longer needed for external reference.
   145	5. **Document.**  Add a docstring to the shared helper citing the paper or
   146	   blueprint location it supports.
   147	
   148	### Legacy identifier treatment
   149	
   150	If a docstring must mention a legacy Lean identifier, cite it in backticks and
   151	describe the mathematical object in paper terminology. If an old public
   152	identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR, record the required migration
   153	in the issue, PR description, or an audit file under `audits/`.
   154	
   155	Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
   156	public name.  This is different from a documented public wrapper allowed in the
   157	shared-helper procedure above: a wrapper must preserve a paper-facing or
   158	blueprint-facing term and must say why the alias exists.

item.text: One subtlety in the final comparison is the global-answer encoding: a default relabeling can be faithful only if the source theorem is explicitly about that relabeled POVM. I’m checking the paper’s answer alphabets and theorem notation once more so the review does not mistake a convenient postprocessing for the stated family.

385	    \end{enumerate}
   386	  \end{gamespec}
   387	  \caption{The decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ for the simultaneous low-degree
   388	    test, parameterized by $\ldparams = (q,m,d,\ldc)$.
   389	    The function $\chi(s)$ is defined in \Cref{eq:chi-func}, and $\pi_{i-1}(v)$
   390	    zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$.}
   391	  \label{fig:ld-decider}
   392	\end{figure}
   393	
   394	We define a special class of measurements that are relevant to the soundness
   395	properties of the low-degree test.
   396	
   397	\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]
   398	  \label{def:ld-meas}
   399	  Define $\polymeas{m}{d}{q}$ to be the set of POVM measurements whose outcomes
   400	  correspond to (individual) degree-$d$ polynomials of $m$ variables over
   401	  $\F_q$.
   402	  More generally, for an integer $\ldc$ and tuples $m=(m_1, m_2, \ldots,
   403	  m_\ldc)$, $d=(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_\ldc)$ and $q=(q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_\ldc)$,
   404	  we let $\simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}$ be the set of measurements $G =
   405	  \{G_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_\ldc}\}$ such that for $i\in\{1, 2, \ldots,
   406	  \ldc\}$, $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i:\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \rightarrow
   407	  \F_{q_i}$ with individual degree $d_i$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-encoding} for a definition of individual degree). 
   408	\end{definition}
   409	
   410	Quantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \emph{total} degree was claimed
   411	in~\cite{natarajan2018low}, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test in~\cite{vidick2016three}. Unfortunately there is a gap in the soundness analysis of this test. For our construction we use the low individual degree test, whose quantum soundness is shown in~\cite{ML20} and generalized in~\cite{ji2021quantum}. We state the result in the form that is most directly useful for us, and show how the stated result follows from~\cite{ji2021quantum}.
   412	
   413	\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low-degree test]
   414	  \label{lem:ld-soundness}
   415	  There exists a function $\delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc) = a (dm \ldc)^a (\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ for universal constants $a\geq 1$ and $0<b\leq 1$ 
   416	such that the following
   417	  holds.
   418	  For all $\eps > 0$ and parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$, for all
   419	  projective strategies $(\psi,A,B)$ that succeed with probability at least
   420	  $1-\eps$ in the game $\game^\ld_\ldparams$, there exists measurements
   421	  \[G^w \in \simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}\] on $\mH_w$, for
   422	  $w\in\{\alice,\bob\}$, such that
   423	  \begin{equation*}
   424	    \begin{split}
   425	      A^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}
   426	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   427	      G^\bob_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}\;,\\
   428	      G^\alice_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}
   429	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   430				 B^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}\;,\\
   431	      G^\alice_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}
   432	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   433	      G^\bob_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}\;,
   434	    \end{split}
   435	  \end{equation*}
   436	  where $\delta_{\ld} = \delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc)$, 
   437	  and all three statements are with respect to the state $\ket{\psi}$.
   438	In addition, the first two approximations hold under the uniform distribution over $u\in \F_q^m$,
   439		whereas there is no question distribution associated with the third approximation.
   440	\end{theorem}
   441	
   442	\begin{proof}
   443	Let $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
   444	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
   445	and $m$ divides $q$. Let $\Sigma=\F_q$. Let $\code \subseteq \Sigma^q$ be the Reed-Solomon code with degree $d$. Explicitly, $\code$ is the set of all $(p(x_1),\ldots,p(x_n))$ where $p:\F_q\to\F_q$ is a univariate polynomial of degree at most $d$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ are an enumeration of $\F_q$. Then in the (standard) notation from~\cite{ji2021quantum} $\code$ is a linear $[q,d+1,n-d+1]_\Sigma$ code.
   446	
   447	Observe that the two-prover tensor code test, for the code $\code^{\otimes m}$, as described in~\cite[Figure 1 and Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}, is identical to the game $\game^\ld$ with parameters $\ldparams$ and $\ldc=1$, whose decider is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}. This is because 
   448	\begin{enumerate}

   512	\subsection{The Magic Square game}
   513	\label{sec:ms}
   514	
   515	We recall the \emph{Magic Square game} of Mermin and
   516	Peres~\cite{mermin1990simple,peres1990incompatible,aravind2002simple}.
   517	The Magic Square game is a simple self-test for EPR pairs (it tests for two of
   518	them). In addition, it allows one to test that a pair of observables
   519	\emph{anticommutes}.
   520	Here we use it as a building block to construct the quantum low-degree test. 
   521	
   522	There are several formulations of the Magic Square game; here we present it as a
   523	\emph{binary constraint satisfaction} game~\cite{cleve2014characterization}.
   524	In this formulation of the game (denoted by $\game_\MS$) there are $6$ linear
   525	equations defined over $9$ variables that take values in $\F_2$.
   526	The variables correspond to the cells of a $3 \times 3$ grid, as depicted in
   527	Figure~\ref{fig:ms}.
   528	Five of the equations correspond to the constraint that the sum of the variables
   529	in each row and the first two columns must be equal to $0$, and the last
   530	equation requires that the sum of the variables in the last column must be equal
   531	to $1$.
